title: Slab-built garden stepping stones
subtitle: Three round textured stepping stone discs in grogged air-dry clay, sealed for light outdoor use
excerpt: Garden stepping stones are thick round clay discs with pressed surface texture, made from a grogged air-dry clay body that resists cracking better than standard clay on larger flat pieces. No kiln is required. Each disc is 22 cm in diameter and 20 mm thick, sealed with exterior varnish for light path use.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles for grogged air-dry clay garden work.

glossaryTerms.definition: Clay mixed with fired particles called grog, which reduce shrinkage and cracking on larger flat pieces; available as a ready-mixed air-dry product

content.text: Garden stepping stones are thick round
slab
discs for placing on a path or in a lawn. This version uses a
grogged clay

body and exterior varnish sealing for light outdoor use: the discs handle occasional foot traffic but are not equivalent to fired ceramic pavers. Each disc is 22 cm in diameter and 20 mm thick. A batch of three covers a short path.

materials.name: Grogged air-dry clay (or standard air-dry clay mixed with 20% sharp sand for comparable body texture)
PVA glue diluted 50/50 with water (base seal coat)
Exterior-grade waterproof varnish or masonry sealant spray
Leaves, seed heads, or lace fabric for texture impressions (optional)

tools.name: Pottery rolling pin (or a smooth glass bottle)

content.text: Preparation

Grogged air-dry clay is widely available from ceramic suppliers. If using standard air-dry clay, knead in a handful of sharp sand or fine horticultural grit (roughly 20% by volume) until evenly distributed: this mimics the effect of grog and reduces cracking on thick flat pieces. Make one disc at a time. Each disc requires 500 g of clay and its own drying time before moving on. Roll on a sheet of heavy canvas or a cloth-covered board: the canvas can be peeled away after rolling without distorting the disc.
Rolling and cutting each disc
Take 500 g of clay and flatten into a rough circle by hand before rolling. This prevents air pockets forming under the rolling pin.
Place two 20 mm guide rods (thick wooden dowels or two stacked craft sticks) either side of the clay. Roll the clay to an even 20 mm thickness by rolling the pin across the guide rods.

Press any texture impressions into the top surface now while the clay is fully soft. Lay a large leaf face-down on the clay, roll lightly over it with the rolling pin, then peel away to leave the impression. For lace texture, press a piece of lace fabric with a flat hand, then lift carefully.

Place a 22 cm round template (a dinner plate, a bowl, or a cut paper circle) on the clay surface. Cut around the template with the fettling knife in a single decisive stroke per section. Remove the excess clay from around the disc.
Smooth the cut edge of the disc with a damp pottery sponge. Bevel the edge slightly inward toward the base: a chamfered edge is less likely to chip than a sharp 90-degree edge.
Use the needle tool to scratch your initials or a date into the underside of the disc. Press at least 2 mm deep so the mark survives the PVA seal coat and remains legible.
Drying each disc
Leave each disc on its canvas on a flat surface to air-dry. Do not move the disc for the first 24 hours: the thick slab is prone to warping if disturbed before
leather-hard

. After 24 hours, flip the disc carefully onto a piece of dry cloth to allow air to reach the underside as well. If the disc shows any signs of curling at the edges, place a flat board and a light weight on top and leave for another 12 hours. Full drying to
bone-dry
takes five to seven days for a 20 mm slab. The disc is bone-dry when it is uniformly pale and sounds hollow when tapped.
Sealing

Sealing is the critical step for outdoor use. Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces including the underside and edges. Allow each coat to dry fully. Once the PVA is fully cured, apply three coats of exterior-grade waterproof varnish or masonry sealant spray, following the product instructions for drying time between coats. The PVA hardens the surface; the exterior varnish provides moisture resistance. These discs are not equivalent to fired and glazed ceramic pavers: they will withstand light foot traffic and occasional rain, but not immersion or heavy frost.
Care

Place the discs on a bed of sand or fine gravel to improve drainage and keep the underside from sitting in standing water. Re-seal each spring with a coat of exterior varnish to maintain moisture resistance. Bring the discs inside over winter in climates with hard frost: air-dry clay is not frost-proof and will eventually fracture if water penetrates the seal, freezes, and expands. In frost-free climates the discs can remain in place year-round.
Variations

Press glass pebbles or smooth garden stones into the soft clay surface before cutting to shape. The embedded stones add texture and survive outdoor conditions better than pressed impressions. Press each stone so its flat underside is flush with the clay surface.
Cut the discs into irregular shapes rather than circles: an irregular oval or kidney shape reads as a natural stepping stone. Use the fettling knife freehand rather than against a template.

Carve a number into each disc and use a set of three as house number pavers at the entrance to a path. Cut each number with the needle tool at the leather-hard stage, 3-4 mm deep, and paint with exterior acrylic paint before sealing.

items.problem: Disc warped upward at the edges during drying
items.cause: The top surface dried faster than the underside, causing differential shrinkage
items.fix: At leather-hard, flip the disc and place a flat board with a light weight on top for 12 hours. If already bone-dry and warped, place face-down on a damp cloth for 20 minutes to re-introduce moisture, then press flat under a weight while it re-dries

items.problem: Large cracks appeared across the disc surface
items.cause: The clay dried too fast, or the clay body had insufficient grog to manage shrinkage
items.fix: Cover with a loose cloth and slow the drying for future pieces. Fill surface cracks at leather-hard with clay paste. If using standard air-dry clay, knead in more sharp sand next time

items.problem: Disc crumbled when stepped on after sealing
items.cause: The disc was too thin; 20 mm is the minimum for foot traffic
items.fix: Make future discs with 20 mm guide rods as rolling guides. A crumbled disc cannot be repaired and should be broken up and discarded

items.problem: Texture impression too faint to see after sealing
items.cause: The impression was too shallow, or the PVA coats filled in the texture
items.fix: Press impressions at least 3 mm deep into the soft clay. Thin the PVA mixture to 30/70 PVA to water for the first seal coat on textured pieces so the texture is not obscured
